Asparagus.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer

Asparagus is one of the finest spring vegetables: a long-lived perennial which gives a fresh, delicate crop just when the garden is short of new green shoots. It is not difficult once established, but it asks for space, clean ground and patience. Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clear perennial weeds thoroughly, improve the soil before planting and do not crop hard while the crowns are young. In return, a good bed can produce spears for many years, followed by tall ferny summer growth which feeds the roots for the next season.

Sow

Apr

Harvest

May – Jun

Depth

1 in.

Row spacing

18 in. between rows; stagger plants in adjacent rows

Yield per mature plant

About 10 spears

Plant spacing

18 in. between plants

First cutting 2 years after planting crowns; 3 years from seed

Recommended varieties
Gijnlim

An early, all-male hybrid producing green spears. A strong first choice for a productive, permanent asparagus bed.

Connover's Colossal

A long-established asparagus with substantial green spears. Keep as the traditional alternative to modern all-male hybrids.

Backlim

An all-male hybrid cropping later than early selections. Plant alongside an earlier variety to spread the asparagus harvest.

Key risks
VIOLET ROOT ROT

Purple fungal growth on roots, with yellowing and dying fern, can indicate violet root rot.

FROST

Young shoots may turn black and die if a severe frost occurs in late spring.

PERENNIAL WEEDS

Couch grass, bindweed and other perennial weeds are a serious long-term problem in asparagus beds.

SLUGS

Spears are gnawed, making them unfit for table use.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
88

Growing guide · Asparagus
Good drainage is essential.

Choose a sunny, sheltered site and enrich the soil with compost or well-rotted manure.

Clear perennial weeds before planting.

A light-excluding mulch for a whole season is worthwhile on badly infested ground.

Plant crowns in early spring.

Delay if the soil is cold and wet; keep bought crowns moist.

Soil & preparation
Choose sunny, sheltered, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure; lime very acid ground if needed. Improve heavy-ground drainage or use a raised bed.
Clear perennial weeds first: their roots are hard to remove once tangled with crowns.
Sowing & planting
1 Prepare a mound

Keep crowns moist. Mound fine soil in the clean, well-drained trench.

2 Spread the roots

Spread roots over the mound, with the crown above the root ends.

3 Cover the roots

Cover roots; leave bud tips visible. Water to settle; keep mulch off growth points.

Trench Dig 12 in. wide and 8 in. deep; centres 18 in. apart. Stagger plants in adjacent trenches.
Initial cover Cover roots; leave bud tips visible

From seed: sow thinly in spring, thin and grow on. Plant into the final bed next spring; cropping starts later than with crowns.

Looking after the crop
Hand-weed or hoe shallowly to protect roots. Water in dry spells, especially while plants establish. Mulch mature beds against weeds, keeping growth points clear. Strong summer ferns build next spring’s reserves.
Each year, mulch established beds with 1–2 in. of compost or well-rotted manure. Tidy and lightly feed with compost before spears appear.
Support tall ferns if needed. Remove berries before they fall and seed into the bed. Let ferns yellow before cutting down; remove diseased growth.
Harvesting & storage
Wait two years after planting crowns, or three years from seed. Let uncut spears form fern to build strong roots.
Cut finger-thick spears by 7 in. tall, about 1 in. below soil, before they turn woody. Use a sharp knife, avoiding nearby shoots. Check every few days in cool weather, daily in warmth.
Cut for six weeks in the first harvest year, then up to eight weeks. Stop by mid-June, sooner if weak, and let later spears form fern.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
VIOLET ROOT ROT	Roots develop purple mould; foliage yellows and dies.	Confirm diagnosis; remove affected crowns and replant on clean ground.
FROST	Young shoots turn black and die after late spring frost.	Remove damaged shoots and cover the bed if hard frost is forecast.
PERENNIAL WEEDS	Couch, bindweed and other perennial weeds invade the crowns.	Clear them before planting; later removal risks crop damage.
SLUGS	Spears are gnawed and become unfit to eat.	Check shoots on damp evenings, hand-pick slugs and encourage natural predators.
Final tips

Treat the bed as a permanent feature: clean ground and patience pay off.

Strong summer fern growth feeds the crowns for next spring.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Growing Techniques 156
89
